Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette: Akira, a 20-year-old African woman and pharmacist in her hometown of Detroit, has been struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a traumatic experience involving torture. The intensity of the trauma has left lasting imprints on Akira's psyche and daily life. The event itself was a harrowing ordeal that involved waterboarding and physical confinement, leading to her developing specific triggers like arguments, loss of autonomy, and exposure to large bodies of water or flooding. Whenever she encounters these triggers, particularly during her shift at the pharmacy, the memories come rushing back with vivid bodily sensations, making it feel as though she is reliving those moments. Akira’s coping mechanisms have become increasingly maladaptive over time. She has started avoiding situations that might bring on nightmares and avoids seeing people who remind her of her captors. This avoidance strategy has also extended to arguments at work and home, where the mere suggestion of conflict sends her into a tailspin of anxiety and distress. Her constant hypervigilance—a core belief rooted in the need for survival—has led her to always identify escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. Akira is certain that if she thinks about the event too much, she will not be able to handle it, which only reinforces her tendency to avoid situations that might trigger these memories. The memory of the torture is fragmented and nonverbal, leaving Akira with a sense that parts are missing and unable to articulate what happened. These incomplete memories often surface in moments of stress or when she’s alone at night, causing her to reenact bodily positions from those frightening events. This reenactment intensifies her hypervigilance and fear, further solidifying her belief that she needs to be constantly on guard. As a result, Akira is plagued by sleep vigilance and constant scanning of her surroundings for signs of danger. She has come to believe that if she doesn’t remain alert at all times, something bad will happen again. This heightened state of fear leads her to avoid places like the pharmacy where large bodies of water or stressful interactions might trigger these feelings. The guilt Akira feels over surviving when others did not exacerbates her negative appraisals and fuels her belief that she deserves to suffer because of what happened. She has started punishing herself through self-blame, further deepening her trauma responses. Over time, this cycle has tightened its grip on Akira’s life. Her relationships with friends and family have been strained due to her constant avoidance behaviors and hypervigilance. Even in the pharmacy, where she once felt secure, she now finds herself constantly looking for escape routes and avoiding interactions that might trigger memories of her torture. What finally brought Akira to seek help was a particularly distressing episode at work, where an argument with a colleague triggered intense flashbacks and panic attacks. She realized that these triggers were becoming more frequent and debilitating, affecting not only her job performance but also her personal relationships. Akira is most afraid that the trauma will continue to control every aspect of her life, making it impossible for her to lead a normal life or find peace. However, she is hopeful that with support and treatment, she can regain some semblance of stability and overcome the overwhelming fear and guilt that have been consuming her.
